vignette:
Leila is a 59-year-old police officer, a married woman who has spent over three decades on the force, and she still cannot sit in the passenger seat of her own car. When her husband drives, she grips the door handle, her eyes scanning the road ahead for any sign of trouble, her own heart pounding so hard she can feel it in her throat. It is that pounding, that familiar surge of adrenaline, that now terrifies her more than any suspect ever did. She had learned to trust her body’s alarms on the job—that spike in heart rate that meant danger was near. But now, that same signal feels like a betrayal. Her body keeps reacting as if she is still in danger, even when she is sitting safely in her own driveway, and she cannot make it stop.

The event that broke this trust happened eighteen months ago, during a routine domestic disturbance call. Leila and her partner arrived at a small apartment to find a man in the grip of a violent rage. He was larger than she was, younger, and when he turned on her, she felt the full weight of his fury. He struck her with a lamp, then with his fists. She remembers the sound of it—the crack of the lamp base against her skull, the wet thud of his knuckles against her jaw. She can still hear those sounds in her head when the memory comes, clear and detailed, as if she is back in that cramped hallway. The terror she felt then returns undiminished, a wave that washes over her without warning. She was saved by her partner’s intervention, but in the months that followed, something inside her shifted permanently.

At first, Leila tried to carry on. She returned to work, but found herself watching every civilian with suspicion. She became hypervigilant for dangerous people, scanning faces in the station, in the grocery store, in her own neighborhood. She began to believe that she could not rely on other people—not her colleagues, not her husband, not anyone. They had not been there when she needed them. The assault felt deeply unfair, and nothing had been done about it. The man was arrested, but the charges were reduced. He served six months. Leila saw no justice. The injustice sat in her chest like a stone, and she carried it everywhere.

To manage the growing dread, Leila started to isolate herself. She stopped answering phone calls from her sisters. She declined invitations to dinner with friends. She told her husband she was tired, that she needed space. Over time, she cut off contact with almost everyone she had known. The only person she still spoke to was her husband, and even that felt strained. She could not explain to him why she flinched when he touched her shoulder, why she insisted on driving everywhere, why she would not let him hold her at night.

The worst part, for Leila, was the feeling that her own mind was turning against her. She began to monitor her thoughts constantly, checking for signs that she was going crazy. Every intrusive memory, every flash of the hallway, every echo of the lamp cracking against her skull—she treated these as evidence that she was losing her grip. She would catch herself thinking about the assault during a quiet moment and immediately try to push it away, as if the thought itself were a symptom of something worse.

Now, nearly a year and a half later, Leila has come to her first appointment because her husband threatened to leave if she did not get help. She is afraid of that, too—afraid of losing the only person she has left, and afraid of what she might become if she is alone. What she hopes for, though she cannot quite say it out loud, is that someone can show her how to stop the pounding in her chest, how to sit still without scanning the room for threats, how to remember what happened without feeling like she is still there, still fighting for her life.
